title: Macroeconomics
tagline: National income in the long run, money and inflation, unemployment, consumption and investment, IS–LM and aggregate demand, aggregate supply and the Phillips curve, stabilisation and public debt
summary: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: output, unemployment, inflation and interest rates, and the policies that affect them. This course builds the standard intermediate models — the classical long-run model, money and inflation, the labour market, consumption and investment, IS–LM, aggregate supply and the Phillips curve — and uses them to analyse stabilisation policy, budget deficits and government debt.
overview: A household choosing how much to save, a firm deciding whether to add a machine, a central bank setting a policy rate, a finance ministry writing a budget: each of those decisions is microeconomic. **Macroeconomics** is what happens when they are added up. The objects of the subject are national totals and averages — output $Y$, consumption $C$, investment $I$, the unemployment rate $u$, the price level $P$ and inflation $\pi$, the real interest rate $r$ and the nominal rate $i$ — together with the government and monetary policies that shift them. This course is the standard intermediate treatment: closed-economy models of the long run and the short run, written so that a student who has done [[principles/measuring-the-macroeconomy]] and the relevant chapters of [[mathematical-economics]] can derive the results rather than only remember the pictures.

The course has three movements. The first is the **classical long-run model**, in which prices and wages are flexible, output is determined by the supply of capital and labour and by technology, and the real interest rate equates saving and investment. Money determines the price level (the quantity theory) and, through the Fisher relation $i \approx r + \pi^e$, the nominal interest rate; unemployment at this horizon is the **natural rate**, generated by job-finding, job-separation and wage-setting frictions rather than by a shortage of demand. The second movement is the **demand side in the short run**: consumption and investment as behavioural relationships, the Keynesian cross and the multiplier, and the IS–LM model of goods- and money-market equilibrium. The third is **aggregate supply, inflation and policy**: the Phillips curve, the AD–AS model, the debate over stabilisation (rules versus discretion, the Lucas critique), and the government budget constraint that links deficits to the path of public debt.

Macroeconomics is a subject with live disagreements. Keynesians, monetarists, new classicals and New Keynesians share a language of national accounts and of $Y$, $r$ and $\pi$, but they disagree about price flexibility, the formation of expectations, the size of multipliers and whether policy can usefully lean against the cycle. This course presents those views on their own terms and keeps positive claims (what a model implies, what a dated study found) separate from normative ones. Where a chapter discusses what policy might do, it sets out the trade-offs and the value judgements involved; it does not conclude for the reader. The material is **for education only — not investment or financial advice**, and it is not a recommendation of any fiscal or monetary programme.

What makes the subject hard is not the algebra — most of the models here are linear or log-linear — but the discipline of matching a model to a question. A classical diagram answers a long-run question about crowding-out; it does not, by itself, answer a short-run question about a recession. Keep the horizon, the price-adjustment assumption and the treatment of expectations in view whenever you shift a curve. Work every numerical example with a pencil; the widgets are there to build intuition, not to replace the derivation. Later courses take the same material further: [[economic-growth]] on the supply side over decades, [[business-cycles]] on the New Keynesian three-equation model, [[international-finance]] on the open economy, and [[money-banking]] on the institutions that supply money and credit.
outcomes: Derive factor prices, factor shares and the real interest rate in the classical closed-economy model, and show how a change in saving, investment demand or government purchases affects them.
Apply the quantity theory and the Fisher relation $i \approx r + \pi^e$ to inflation, nominal interest rates and seigniorage, and distinguish the costs of anticipated and unanticipated inflation.
Compute the natural rate of unemployment from job-finding and job-separation rates, and compare frictional, structural and wage-rigidity accounts of why that rate is positive.
Solve two-period consumption problems, contrast the Keynesian consumption function with the permanent-income and life-cycle hypotheses, and state the conditions for Ricardian equivalence.
Determine the desired capital stock from the user cost of capital and explain how Tobin’s $q$, residential investment and inventories respond to the real interest rate and to output.
Derive the IS and LM schedules, compute the goods-market multiplier, and analyse fiscal and monetary policy in IS–LM, including the liquidity-trap case.
Connect short-run aggregate supply to the Phillips curve, and compute the inflation path and the output cost of a disinflation under adaptive and rational expectations.
Use the AD–AS model to trace demand and supply shocks, and evaluate the rules-versus-discretion debate and the Lucas critique as positive arguments about policy design.
Iterate the government budget constraint, describe the dynamics of the debt-to-GDP ratio, and set out competing views of the burden of public debt without treating any of them as a recommendation.

chapters.title: National income in the long run
chapters.summary: Output, factor prices and the distribution of income in the classical model, and how saving and investment determine the real interest rate.

chapters.title: Money and inflation
chapters.summary: The quantity theory of money, seigniorage, the Fisher effect, the costs of inflation and hyperinflation.

chapters.title: Unemployment and the labour market
chapters.summary: Job finding and job separation, the natural rate of unemployment, frictional and structural unemployment, and wage rigidity.

chapters.title: Consumption and saving
chapters.summary: From the Keynesian consumption function to intertemporal choice, the permanent-income and life-cycle hypotheses, and Ricardian equivalence.

chapters.title: Investment
chapters.summary: Business fixed investment and the user cost of capital, Tobin’s q, residential investment and inventories.

chapters.title: Aggregate demand: the IS–LM model
chapters.summary: The Keynesian cross, equilibrium in the goods and money markets, and the effects of fiscal and monetary policy on output and interest rates.

chapters.title: Aggregate supply and the Phillips curve
chapters.summary: Short-run aggregate supply, sticky prices and wages, the Phillips curve, expectations and the costs of disinflation.

chapters.title: Stabilisation policy
chapters.summary: The AD–AS model in action, demand and supply shocks, policy lags, rules versus discretion, and the Lucas critique.

chapters.title: Fiscal policy and government debt
chapters.summary: Budget deficits, the government budget constraint, the dynamics of the debt ratio, and the debate over the burden of public debt.

history.title: Fisher’s quantity theory
history.detail: Irving Fisher’s The Purchasing Power of Money restated the equation of exchange $MV = PY$ as a theory of the price level, with $V$ treated as institutionally determined in the long run. The book is the classical source for the quantity theory used in this course.

history.title: Keynes’s General Theory
history.detail: John Maynard Keynes’s The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money argued that, with sticky wages and a consumption function driven by current income, aggregate demand can determine output in the short run. The book set the agenda for the models of consumption, the multiplier and IS–LM that follow.

history.title: Hicks and IS–LM
history.detail: John Hicks’s paper “Mr. Keynes and the Classics” (Econometrica) translated Keynes’s argument into two schedules in $(Y, r)$ space: investment–saving (IS) and liquidity–money (LM). IS–LM became the workhorse of intermediate macroeconomics.

history.title: Friedman’s consumption function
history.detail: Milton Friedman’s A Theory of the Consumption Function proposed that households consume out of permanent rather than current income. Together with the Modigliani–Brumberg life-cycle hypothesis, it replaced the simple Keynesian consumption function as the benchmark intertemporal theory.

history.title: The Phillips curve
history.detail: A. W. Phillips plotted a century of U.K. data and reported a negative association between unemployment and the rate of change of money wages (Economica). Samuelson and Solow (1960) drew an American analogue in inflation–unemployment space, which became the policy trade-off of the 1960s.

history.title: The natural-rate hypothesis
history.detail: Milton Friedman’s presidential address to the American Economic Association, “The Role of Monetary Policy”, argued that the Phillips curve is vertical in the long run at the natural rate of unemployment. Edmund Phelps reached a closely related conclusion in work published in 1967–68.

history.title: The Lucas critique
history.detail: Robert Lucas’s “Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique” argued that estimated policy multipliers are not invariant to the policy rule, because private agents’ expectations adjust. The paper is the founding document of the rational-expectations approach to policy evaluation.

history.title: Rules rather than discretion
history.detail: Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott’s “Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans” (Journal of Political Economy) showed that a policymaker who re-optimises every period has an inflationary bias. The result is the modern case for commitment in monetary policy.

history.title: The Taylor rule
history.detail: John Taylor’s “Discretion versus Policy Rules in Practice” proposed a simple interest-rate rule that raises the real policy rate when inflation is above target or output is above potential. The rule became the benchmark description of how inflation-targeting central banks set rates.

references.title: Macroeconomics
references.note: The standard intermediate textbook (11th ed.). Closest in organisation to this course; especially clear on the classical model, IS–LM and the Phillips curve.

references.title: Macroeconomics
references.note: The other widely used intermediate text (8th ed.), organised around the IS–LM–PC model and unusually careful about the distinction between the short, medium and long run.

references.title: Macroeconomics: Institutions, Instability, and the Financial System
references.note: A 3-equation (IS–PC–MR) treatment that puts the financial system and the zero lower bound into the intermediate course rather than leaving them for later.

references.title: Macroeconomics
references.note: A growth-first intermediate book (5th ed.) with a clean treatment of the long run and of the data; a useful companion to the classical chapters here.

references.title: Advanced Macroeconomics
references.note: The graduate sequel (5th ed.). Use it when you want the microfoundations of consumption, investment, the New Keynesian model or debt dynamics in full.

references.title: Monetary Theory and Policy
references.note: A rigorous treatment (4th ed.) of money demand, inflation, interest-rate rules and the New Keynesian model; the natural next step after the monetary chapters of this course.
